claim: At least two types of RNP granules populate the germ plasm, a cytoplasmic domain at the posterior of the Drosophila oocyte and embryo.
source: At least two types of RNP granules populate the germ plasm, a cytoplasmic domain at the posterior of the Drosophila oocyte and embryo.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's description of germ granules and founder granules as distinct RNP granule types in the germ plasm, with experimental data showing their different compositions and behaviors.

claim: Germ granules deliver mRNAs required for germline development to pole cells, the germ cell progenitors.
source: Germ granules deliver mRNAs required for germline development to pole cells, the germ cell progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established knowledge about germ granule function and data showing germ granule mRNAs are maintained and enriched in pole cells.

claim: Founder granules contain oskar mRNA, which encodes the germ plasm organizer.
source: A second type of RNP granule, here named founder granules, contains oskar mRNA, which encodes the germ plasm organizer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oskar mRNA localization in distinct RNP bodies separate from germ granules.

claim: oskar mRNA is essential for germ plasm assembly during oogenesis.
source: Whereas oskar mRNA is essential for germ plasm assembly during oogenesis, we show that it is toxic to pole cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations to previous work on oskar function.

claim: oskar mRNA is toxic to pole cells.
source: Whereas oskar mRNA is essential for germ plasm assembly during oogenesis, we show that it is toxic to pole cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that untranslatable oskar mRNA targeted to pole cells impairs pole cell formation and migration.

claim: Founder granules mediate compartmentalized degradation of oskar during embryogenesis to minimize its inheritance by pole cells.
source: Founder granules mediate compartmentalized degradation of oskar during embryogenesis to minimize its inheritance by pole cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oskar degradation occurs within founder granules and reduces oskar levels before pole cell formation.

claim: Degradation of oskar in founder granules is temporally and mechanistically distinct from degradation of oskar and other mRNAs during the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
source: Degradation of oskar in founder granules is temporally and mechanistically distinct from degradation of oskar and other mRNAs during the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different timing of degradation and different requirements for degradation factors between germ plasm and bulk cytoplasm oskar.

claim: Compartmentalization in RNP granules differentially controls fates of mRNAs localized within the same cytoplasmic domain.
source: Our results show how compartmentalization in RNP granules differentially controls fates of mRNAs localized within the same cytoplasmic domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oskar in founder granules is degraded while nanos in germ granules is stable, despite both being in the germ plasm.

claim: Drosophila has relatively late zygotic genome activation and consequent reliance on maternally synthesized transcripts.
source: Due in part to its relatively late zygotic genome activation (ZGA) and consequent reliance on maternally synthesized transcripts, Drosophila has served as a valuable model for studying post-transcriptional gene regulation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Mechanisms including mRNA localization, translational control, and mRNA degradation are critical for establishing the body axes in Drosophila.
source: Mechanisms including mRNA localization, translational control, and mRNA degradation are critical for establishing the body axes, for germline development, and for the elimination of maternal transcripts during the maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT) when maternal products are replaced by zygotic gene products.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and citations to previous work.

claim: RNP granules serve to compartmentalize regulatory events within the cytoplasm.
source: These non-membrane bound bodies serve to compartmentalize regulatory events within the cytoplasm, such as sequestration of translationally repressed mRNAs in stress granules and P bodies (Guzikowski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RNP granules can promote colocalization and co-regulation of mRNAs that function in the same biological process.
source: RNP granules can also promote colocalization and co-regulation of mRNAs that function in the same biological process and the segregation of different mRNAs with conflicting regulatory needs (Buchan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Hundreds of mRNAs are highly enriched in the germ plasm.
source: Hundreds of mRNAs are highly enriched in the germ plasm, a specialized cytoplasm that forms at the posterior of the Drosophila oocyte and persists in the early embryo, where it induces the formation of the germ cell progenitors, called pole cells, and specifies germline fate (Jambor et al., 2015; Lécuyer et al., 2007; Mahowald, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The germ plasm induces the formation of pole cells and specifies germline fate.
source: Hundreds of mRNAs are highly enriched in the germ plasm, a specialized cytoplasm that forms at the posterior of the Drosophila oocyte and persists in the early embryo, where it induces the formation of the germ cell progenitors, called pole cells, and specifies germline fate (Jambor et al., 2015; Lécuyer et al., 2007; Mahowald, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many germ plasm mRNAs are co-packaged in RNP assemblies called germ granules.
source: Many of these mRNAs are co-packaged in RNP assemblies called germ granules, which coordinate their segregation to the transcriptionally quiescent pole cells (Lerit and Gavis, 2011; Little et al., 2015; Trcek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Germ granules coordinate segregation of mRNAs to transcriptionally quiescent pole cells.
source: Many of these mRNAs are co-packaged in RNP assemblies called germ granules, which coordinate their segregation to the transcriptionally quiescent pole cells (Lerit and Gavis, 2011; Little et al., 2015; Trcek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: nanos mRNA functions in germline development.
source: Among these are mRNAs like nanos that function in germline development (Kobayashi et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: oskar encodes a core germ granule protein whose synthesis at the posterior of the oocyte initiates germ plasm assembly.
source: One such transcript, oskar, encodes a core germ granule protein whose synthesis at the posterior of the oocyte initiates germ plasm assembly.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about oskar function.

claim: Production of Oskar is targeted to the posterior of the oocyte by transport of oskar mRNA to the posterior, where its translation is activated.
source: Production of Oskar is targeted to the posterior of the oocyte by transport of oskar mRNA to the posterior, where its translation is activated.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about oskar regulation.

claim: Oskar protein nucleates formation of germ granules with the recruitment of additional core granule proteins.
source: Oskar protein then nucleates formation of germ granules with the recruitment of additional core granule proteins (Lehmann, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: nanos and numerous other transcripts populate the germ granules as oogenesis progresses.
source: As oogenesis progresses, nanos and numerous other transcripts populate the germ granules (Forrest and Gavis, 2003; Little et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: oskar mRNA is not incorporated into germ granules but forms large RNP bodies together with Staufen.
source: By contrast, oskar mRNA is not incorporated into germ granules but forms large RNP bodies, together with the double-stranded RNA-binding protein Staufen, that contain several to hundreds of oskar transcripts (Little et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: oskar-containing RNP bodies contain several to hundreds of oskar transcripts.
source: By contrast, oskar mRNA is not incorporated into germ granules but forms large RNP bodies, together with the double-stranded RNA-binding protein Staufen, that contain several to hundreds of oskar transcripts (Little et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Germ plasm formation begins with oskar mRNA localization.
source: Because germ plasm formation begins with oskar mRNA localization (Lehmann, 2016), we refer to the oskar-containing RNPs in the germ plasm as founder granules.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Localized oskar transcripts represent only 18% of total oskar in the embryo.
source: Notably, although both germ granule destined mRNAs and oskar are highly enriched in the germ plasm by virtue of their respective granule association, the localized transcripts represent only a small fraction of their total masses in the embryo (≤4% and 18%, respectively) (Bergsten and Gavis, 1999; Little et al., 2015; Trcek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Localized germ granule mRNAs represent ≤4% of their total mass in the embryo.
source: Notably, although both germ granule destined mRNAs and oskar are highly enriched in the germ plasm by virtue of their respective granule association, the localized transcripts represent only a small fraction of their total masses in the embryo (≤4% and 18%, respectively) (Bergsten and Gavis, 1999; Little et al., 2015; Trcek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The majority of oskar and germ granule mRNAs remain distributed throughout the cytoplasm where they are silenced and ultimately degraded during the MZT.
source: The majority remain distributed throughout the cytoplasm, where they are silenced by additional layers of post-transcriptional regulation and ultimately degraded during the MZT.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data about localized vs. total mRNA populations and knowledge about MZT.

claim: The Drosophila embryo develops as a syncytium in which nuclei undergo 13 rounds of semi-synchronous divisions before the major wave of ZGA and cellularization occur.
source: The Drosophila embryo develops as a syncytium in which nuclei undergo 13 rounds of semi-synchronous divisions (nuclear cycles; nc) before the major wave of ZGA and cellularization occur.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Pole cells form precociously during nc10 when cell membrane buds enclose nuclei that have entered the germ plasm.
source: The pole cells form precociously, however, during nc10 when cell membrane buds enclose nuclei that have entered the germ plasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a figure showing developmental timing and by established knowledge.

claim: Both germ granules and founder granules persist in the germ plasm after fertilization.
source: Whereas both germ granules and founder granules persist in the germ plasm after fertilization, only the germ granules become enriched in the pole cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Only germ granules become enriched in pole cells.
source: Whereas both germ granules and founder granules persist in the germ plasm after fertilization, only the germ granules become enriched in the pole cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting oskar to germ granules and consequent accumulation of oskar in pole cells impairs germline development.
source: This distinction is important, as targeting oskar to germ granules and consequent accumulation of oskar in pole cells impairs germline development, decreasing the number of pole cells formed and disrupting their migration to the gonad during gastrulation (Little et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Targeting oskar to germ granules decreases the number of pole cells formed.
source: This distinction is important, as targeting oskar to germ granules and consequent accumulation of oskar in pole cells impairs germline development, decreasing the number of pole cells formed and disrupting their migration to the gonad during gastrulation (Little et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Targeting oskar to germ granules disrupts pole cell migration to the gonad during gastrulation.
source: This distinction is important, as targeting oskar to germ granules and consequent accumulation of oskar in pole cells impairs germline development, decreasing the number of pole cells formed and disrupting their migration to the gonad during gastrulation (Little et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: oskar mRNA itself, and not its capacity to produce Oskar protein, is toxic to pole cells.
source: We now report that oskar mRNA itself, and not its capacity to produce Oskar protein, is toxic to pole cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing untranslatable oskar mRNA causes pole cell defects.

claim: oskar is degraded in the germ plasm beginning in nc7.
source: We show that, in contrast to germ granule mRNAs, oskar is degraded in the germ plasm beginning in nc7.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oskar levels decrease starting at nc7.

claim: Germ granule mRNAs are not degraded in the germ plasm during pole cell formation.
source: We show that, in contrast to germ granule mRNAs, oskar is degraded in the germ plasm beginning in nc7.
evidence: This claim is implied by the contrast with oskar degradation and supported by data showing nanos stability.

claim: Selectivity of oskar degradation occurs through the recruitment of mRNA decay factors specifically by founder granules.
source: This selectivity occurs through the recruitment of mRNA decay factors specifically by founder granules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing DCP1 colocalizes with oskar in founder granules but not with germ granule mRNAs.

claim: Degradation of oskar results in founder granule destabilization.
source: The subsequent degradation of oskar results in founder granule destabilization and ultimately limits uptake of oskar by pole cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing founder granule size and Staufen content decrease after oskar degradation.

claim: Founder granule destabilization limits uptake of oskar by pole cells.
source: The subsequent degradation of oskar results in founder granule destabilization and ultimately limits uptake of oskar by pole cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing oskar degradation reduces oskar available for pole cell incorporation.

claim: Founder granules promote oskar degradation in the germ plasm well in advance of the degradation of unlocalized oskar during the MZT.
source: Founder granules impart another level of spatiotemporal control by promoting oskar degradation in the germ plasm well in advance of the degradation of unlocalized oskar during the MZT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing germ plasm oskar degradation begins at nc7 while bulk cytoplasm oskar degradation begins at nc11.

claim: Degradation of oskar in the germ plasm occurs by a process distinct from the degradation of unlocalized oskar during the MZT.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that degradation of oskar in the germ plasm occurs by a process distinct from the degradation of unlocalized oskar during the MZT and requires the Piwi protein Aubergine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different factor requirements for germ plasm vs. bulk cytoplasm oskar degradation.

claim: Degradation of oskar in the germ plasm requires the Piwi protein Aubergine.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that degradation of oskar in the germ plasm occurs by a process distinct from the degradation of unlocalized oskar during the MZT and requires the Piwi protein Aubergine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oskar is stabilized in aubergine mutants.

claim: oM1,139R∆n mRNA colocalized with germ granules and was incorporated into pole cells.
source: Similarly to o∆n mRNA, oM1,139R∆n colocalized with germ granules and was incorporated into pole cells (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-F.

claim: Embryos from females expressing oM1,139R∆n formed fewer pole cells than wild-type embryos.
source: Like embryos from females expressing o∆n, embryos from females expressing oM1,139R∆n formed fewer pole cells than wild-type embryos (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: oM1,139R∆n embryos showed pole cell migration defects similar to those of o∆n embryos.
source: The oM1,139R∆n embryos also showed pole cell migration defects similar to those of o∆n embryos, with many pole cells failing to reach the gonad (Figure 1K–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1K-M.

claim: Mis-incorporation of oskar mRNA itself in germ granules interferes with germline development, independently of Oskar protein production.
source: Thus, mis-incorporation of oskar mRNA itself in germ granules interferes with germline development, independently of Oskar protein production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing untranslatable oskar causes pole cell defects.

claim: The toxicity of oskar mRNA could result from titration of one or more factors involved in germline development.
source: The toxicity of oskar mRNA could result from titration of one or more factors involved in germline development, similarly to the proposed noncoding function of oskar during oogenesis (Jenny et al., 2006; Kanke et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on analogy to previous work.

claim: Only low levels of oskar are detected in pole cells in wild-type embryos.
source: In wild-type embryos, only low levels of oskar are detected in pole cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Germ granules become enriched in pole cells by virtue of their accumulation at centrosomes associated with posterior nuclei.
source: Germ granules become enriched in the pole cells by virtue of their accumulation at centrosomes associated with posterior nuclei.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: Germ granule accumulation at centrosomes occurs by dynein-mediated transport on astral microtubules.
source: This accumulation occurs by dynein-mediated transport on astral microtubules and triggers the budding of the plasma membrane around the nuclei and associated germ granules to form the pole cells (Lerit and Gavis, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During mid-oogenesis, oskar RNPs are transported to the posterior of the oocyte by kinesin.
source: During mid-oogenesis, oskar RNPs are transported to the posterior of the oocyte by kinesin (Brendza et al., 2000; Gáspár et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Germ granules exhibited directed motility toward embryonic nuclei at the onset of pole cell formation.
source: As previously observed (Lerit and Gavis, 2011), germ granules exhibited directed motility toward embryonic nuclei at the onset of pole cell formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and current observations.

claim: Most founder granules appeared to jiggle in place during pole cell formation.
source: By contrast, most founder granules appeared to jiggle in place (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Video 1.

claim: Founder granules moved more slowly, with smaller displacements, and with fewer linear trajectories than germ granules.
source: Tracking of both germ granules and founder granules showed that founder granules moved more slowly, with smaller displacements, and with fewer linear trajectories than germ granules (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Germ granules became clustered around nuclei as a result of their directed motility.
source: Whereas germ granules became clustered around nuclei as a result of their directed motility, the less motile founder granules remained uniformly distributed in the germ plasm (Figure 2E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E-I.

claim: Founder granules remained uniformly distributed in the germ plasm during pole cell formation.
source: Whereas germ granules became clustered around nuclei as a result of their directed motility, the less motile founder granules remained uniformly distributed in the germ plasm (Figure 2E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E-I.

claim: Founder granules were detected among the germ granules clustered around nuclei and near the cortex.
source: Consequently, founder granules were detected among the germ granules clustered around nuclei (Figure 2F,H) and near the cortex (Figure 2H,I), suggesting that they can be passively incorporated in pole cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F, H, I.

claim: Founder granules can be passively incorporated in pole cells.
source: Consequently, founder granules were detected among the germ granules clustered around nuclei (Figure 2F,H) and near the cortex (Figure 2H,I), suggesting that they can be passively incorporated in pole cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that founder granules are present near forming pole cells.

claim: Since founder granules do not disperse from the vicinity of the forming pole cells, uptake of oskar by pole cells must be limited by another mechanism.
source: Moreover, since founder granules do not disperse from the vicinty of the forming pole cells, uptake of oskar by pole cells must be limited by another mechanism.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that founder granules remain near pole cells but oskar levels in pole cells are low.

claim: The amount of oskar mRNA in the germ plasm decreased by 98% from before pole cell formation to after pole cell formation.
source: As measured by total fluorescence intensity, the amount of oskar mRNA in the germ plasm decreased by 98% from before pole cell formation to after pole cell formation (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, C.

claim: There was no significant change in the amount of nanos in the germ plasm during pole cell formation.
source: Consistent with previous studies showing that germ granule mRNAs are maintained in the germ plasm throughout pole cell formation (Bashirullah et al., 2001), there was no significant change in the amount of nanos (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C and citation to previous work.

claim: The amount of germ plasm localized og mRNA decreased by 90% from before to after pole cell formation.
source: FISH analysis showed that the amount of germ plasm localized og mRNA decreased by 90% from before to after pole cell formation, whereas o∆gn mRNA remained largely unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: o∆gn mRNA remained largely unchanged during pole cell formation.
source: FISH analysis showed that the amount of germ plasm localized og mRNA decreased by 90% from before to after pole cell formation, whereas o∆gn mRNA remained largely unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sizes of founder granules decreased over the course of pole cell formation.
source: In addition to oskar mRNA levels, the sizes of founder granules, as measured by the number of oskar mRNAs they contain (see Materials and methods), decreased over the course of pole cell formation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Germ granule size distributions were unchanged during pole cell formation.
source: By contrast, germ granule size distributions, measured by the number of nanos transcripts they contain, were unchanged (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: mRNA degradation typically involves removal of the 5' cap followed by exonuclease digestion.
source: mRNA degradation typically involves removal of the 5' cap followed by exonuclease digestion.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about mRNA degradation mechanisms.

claim: In Drosophila, decapping is carried out by Decapping Protein 2 (DCP2) and its cofactor Decapping Protein 1 (DCP1).
source: In Drosophila, decapping is carried out by Decapping Protein 2 (DCP2) and its cofactor Decapping Protein 1 (DCP1) (Siwaszek et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The frequency of detecting oskar particles colocalized with DCP1 began to increase at nc5 and continued to increase through pole cell formation.
source: Within the germ plasm, the frequency of detecting a particle containing one or more oskar transcripts colocalized with DCP1 began to increase at nc5 and continued to increase through pole cell formation (Figure 4A–C and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: DCP1 did not colocalize with cyclin B, a representative germ granule mRNA.
source: Consistent with the differential stability of oskar and germ granule mRNAs in the germ plasm, we did not detect colocalization of DCP1 with a representative germ granule mRNA, cyclin B (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 77% of oskar particles that colocalized with DCP1 also colocalized with Me31B.
source: In addition, we found that 77% and 49% of oskar particles that colocalized with DCP1 also colocalized with the decapping complex associated protein Me31B (Figure 4D,D',F) and the 5' to 3' exonuclease Pacman (Figure 4E,E',G), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D, D', F.

claim: 49% of oskar particles that colocalized with DCP1 also colocalized with Pacman.
source: In addition, we found that 77% and 49% of oskar particles that colocalized with DCP1 also colocalized with the decapping complex associated protein Me31B (Figure 4D,D',F) and the 5' to 3' exonuclease Pacman (Figure 4E,E',G), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E, E', G.

claim: Recruitment of Pacman was delayed relative to DCP1.
source: Temporal analysis showed that recruitment of Pacman was delayed relative to DCP1 (Figure 4C), indicating that the degradation machinery is recruited in a sequential manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The degradation machinery is recruited to founder granules in a sequential manner.
source: Temporal analysis showed that recruitment of Pacman was delayed relative to DCP1 (Figure 4C), indicating that the degradation machinery is recruited in a sequential manner.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal data on DCP1 and Pacman recruitment.

claim: DCP1 did not colocalize with o∆gn mRNA in germ granules.
source: Notably, DCP1 did not colocalize with o∆gn mRNA in germ granules (Figure 4H–I), suggesting that the degradation machinery is specifically recruited to founder granule associated oskar.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: The degradation machinery is specifically recruited to founder granule associated oskar.
source: Notably, DCP1 did not colocalize with o∆gn mRNA in germ granules (Figure 4H–I), suggesting that the degradation machinery is specifically recruited to founder granule associated oskar.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential colocalization of DCP1 with oskar in founder granules vs. germ granules.

claim: oskar degradation dramatically reduces the amount of oskar mRNA available for incorporation into pole cells.
source: We conclude that oskar degradation dramatically reduces the amount of oskar mRNA available for incorporation into pole cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing oskar degradation before pole cell formation.

claim: 35.0 ± 5.9% of Staufen particles that colocalized with oskar were also colocalized with DCP1 at nuclear cycle 8.
source: This analysis revealed that 35.0 ± 5.9% of Staufen particles that colocalized with oskar were also colocalized with DCP1 at nuclear cycle 8 (data not shown), consistent with the measurement for oskar mRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data mentioned in the text.

claim: 90.0 ± 5.4% of DCP1 particles colocalized with Staufen were also colocalized with oskar.
source: Of the DCP1 particles colocalized with Staufen, 90.0 ± 5.4% were also colocalized with oskar (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data mentioned in the text.

claim: DCP1 associates with intact founder granules.
source: Thus, DCP1 associates with intact founder granules.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the colocalization data showing DCP1 with both oskar and Staufen.

claim: DCP1 associated with oskar particles of all sizes.
source: However, we found that DCP1 associated with oskar particles of all sizes (Figure 5G,H) suggesting that oskar mRNA is not released from founder granules prior to the onset of degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G, H.

claim: oskar mRNA is not released from founder granules prior to the onset of degradation.
source: However, we found that DCP1 associated with oskar particles of all sizes (Figure 5G,H) suggesting that oskar mRNA is not released from founder granules prior to the onset of degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that DCP1 associates with oskar particles of all sizes.

claim: The 5':3' ratio of oskar fluorescence decreased significantly between nc3-4 and nc7-8 for both larger and smaller particles.
source: For both larger and smaller particles, the 5':3' ratio decreased significantly between nc3-4 and nc7-8, reflecting the loss of sequences from the 5' end of oskar (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The decrease in 5':3' ratio reflects the loss of sequences from the 5' end of oskar.
source: For both larger and smaller particles, the 5':3' ratio decreased significantly between nc3-4 and nc7-8, reflecting the loss of sequences from the 5' end of oskar (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the 5' to 3' directionality of mRNA degradation and the observed ratio change.

claim: oskar degradation occurs within founder granules.
source: Together, the data presented here support a model in which oskar degradation occurs within founder granules.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including timing, colocalization, and 5':3' ratio data.

claim: Colocalization of oskar with DCP1 first began to increase at nc5.
source: As described above, colocalization of oskar with DCP1 first began to increase at nc5 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The amount of oskar in the germ plasm decreased subsequently at nc7.
source: The amount of oskar in the germ plasm decreased subsequently at nc7 (Figure 5A), and the average size of oskar particles declined sharply at nc9, when pole cells form (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The average size of oskar particles declined sharply at nc9, when pole cells form.
source: The amount of oskar in the germ plasm decreased subsequently at nc7 (Figure 5A), and the average size of oskar particles declined sharply at nc9, when pole cells form (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The amount of Staufen in founder granules began to decrease at nc11.
source: The amount of Staufen in founder granules, measured by immunofluorescence intensity, began to decrease at nc11 (Figure 5C) along with a dramatic decrease in the percentage of Staufen particles that remained associated with oskar (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was a dramatic decrease in the percentage of Staufen particles that remained associated with oskar at nc11.
source: The amount of Staufen in founder granules, measured by immunofluorescence intensity, began to decrease at nc11 (Figure 5C) along with a dramatic decrease in the percentage of Staufen particles that remained associated with oskar (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The order of events is consistent with association of the degradation factors with intact founder granules leading to oskar degradation, followed by the destabilization of founder granules.
source: This order of events is consistent with association of the degradation factors with intact founder granules leading to oskar degradation, followed by the destabilization of founder granules.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal sequence of DCP1 recruitment, oskar degradation, particle size decrease, and Staufen loss.

claim: The percentage of oskar particles colocalized with Staufen remained unchanged until nc10.
source: Furthermore, the percentage of oskar particles colocalized with Staufen remained unchanged until nc10, when there was a small decrease in colocalization (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Widespread clearance of maternal mRNAs occurs during the MZT and is controlled by both maternal and zygotic degradation factors.
source: Widespread clearance of maternal mRNAs occurs during the MZT and is controlled by both maternal and zygotic degradation factors.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: The maternal decay machinery is set in motion by egg activation whereas the zygotic pathway is engaged following ZGA.
source: The maternal decay machinery is set in motion by egg activation whereas the zygotic pathway is engaged following ZGA (Laver et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Genome-wide microarray analysis showed that oskar is degraded during the MZT by both maternal and zygotic pathways.
source: Genome-wide microarray analysis showed that oskar is degraded during the MZT by both maternal and zygotic pathways (Thomsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Only 18% of oskar mRNA in the embryo is localized to the germ plasm and packaged in founder granules.
source: However, because only 18% of oskar mRNA in the embryo is localized to the germ plasm and packaged in founder granules (Bergsten and Gavis, 1999; Little et al., 2015), this analysis predominantly measured the unlocalized population of oskar mRNA in the bulk embryonic cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The first significant decrease in germ plasm localized oskar occurred at nc7.
source: The first significant decrease in germ plasm localized oskar occurred at nc7 (Figure 6C), consistent with our analysis of the total amount of localized oskar (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For unlocalized oskar, the first significant decrease occurred at nc11.
source: For unlocalized oskar, the first significant decrease occurred at nc11.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Association of unlocalized oskar with DCP1 is delayed relative to germ plasm localized oskar.
source: Consistent with the temporal difference in degradation of the two oskar populations, association of unlocalized oskar with DCP1 is delayed relative to germ plasm localized oskar (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D, E.

claim: Degradation of oskar in the germ plasm begins well in advance of degradation of oskar during the MZT.
source: Together, these results indicate that degradation of oskar in the germ plasm begins well in advance of degradation of oskar during the MZT.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal data showing germ plasm oskar degradation at nc7 vs. bulk cytoplasm at nc11.

claim: Brain tumor and Pumilio direct clearance of oskar and numerous other maternal mRNAs in the bulk cytoplasm during the MZT.
source: Two RNA-binding proteins, Brain tumor and Pumilio have been shown to direct clearance of oskar and numerous other maternal mRNAs in the bulk cytoplasm during the MZT (Laver et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Piwi protein Aubergine has been implicated in maternal mRNA degradation.
source: The Piwi protein Aubergine has also been implicated (Barckmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In brain tumor and pumilio mutant embryos, oskar was degraded in the germ plasm similarly to wild-type embryos.
source: In brain tumor and pumilio mutant embryos, oskar was degraded in the germ plasm similarly to wild-type embryos (Figure 7A,B,D and data not shown) indicating that Brain tumor and Pumilio do not target oskar for degradation in the germ plasm as they do in the bulk cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A, B, D.

claim: Brain tumor and Pumilio do not target oskar for degradation in the germ plasm as they do in the bulk cytoplasm.
source: In brain tumor and pumilio mutant embryos, oskar was degraded in the germ plasm similarly to wild-type embryos (Figure 7A,B,D and data not shown) indicating that Brain tumor and Pumilio do not target oskar for degradation in the germ plasm as they do in the bulk cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that oskar degradation is normal in brain tumor and pumilio mutants.

claim: oskar was partially stabilized in the germ plasm of aubergine mutant embryos.
source: However, oskar was partially stabilized in the germ plasm of aubergine mutant embryos (Figure 7A,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A, C, D.

claim: oskar was degraded in wild-type unfertilized eggs independently of progression through embryogenesis.
source: Because most aubergine mutant embryos arrest development prior to pole cell formation, we assessed oskar degradation in wild-type unfertilized eggs and found that oskar was degraded independently of progression through embryogenesis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: oskar degradation requires only maternal factors.
source: Thus, oskar degradation requires only maternal factors and the stabilization of oskar observed in aubergine mutant embryos is not simply a consequence of their developmental arrest.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that oskar is degraded in unfertilized eggs.

claim: The stabilization of oskar observed in aubergine mutant embryos is not simply a consequence of their developmental arrest.
source: Thus, oskar degradation requires only maternal factors and the stabilization of oskar observed in aubergine mutant embryos is not simply a consequence of their developmental arrest.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that oskar is degraded in unfertilized eggs.

claim: DCP1 and oskar did not colocalize in the germ plasm of aubergine mutant embryos.
source: Moreover, we found that DCP1 and oskar did not colocalize in the germ plasm of aubergine mutant embryos (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Introduction of a functional gfp-aub transgene into aubergine mutant females rescued both oskar degradation and DCP1 colocalization.
source: Introduction of a functional gfp-aub transgene into aubergine mutant females rescued both oskar degradation and DCP1 colocalization (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Aubergine plays a role in recruitment of DCP1 to founder granules, resulting in decapping and subsequent degradation of oskar.
source: These results suggest a role for Aubergine in recruitment of DCP1 to founder granules, resulting in decapping and subsequent degradation of oskar.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that aubergine mutants lack DCP1 colocalization and oskar degradation.

claim: oskar particle sizes were stabilized in the germ plasm of aubergine mutants.
source: In addition, oskar particle sizes were stabilized in the germ plasm of aubergine mutants (Figure 7H,I), consistent with oskar degradation causing founder granule destabilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7H, I.

claim: oskar degradation causes founder granule destabilization.
source: In addition, oskar particle sizes were stabilized in the germ plasm of aubergine mutants (Figure 7H,I), consistent with oskar degradation causing founder granule destabilization.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between oskar stability and founder granule stability in aubergine mutants.

claim: Founder granules minimize inheritance of oskar by pole cells by recruiting factors for compartmentalized oskar degradation.
source: We show that oskar RNA itself is toxic to pole cells, necessitating an early-acting mechanism to deplete oskar from the germ plasm. Our results indicate that founder granules minimize inheritance of oskar by pole cells by recruiting factors for compartmentalized oskar degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence showing oskar toxicity, degradation in founder granules, and reduced oskar in pole cells.

claim: Founder granule-associated oskar degradation is distinct from degradation of unlocalized oskar, nanos, and other maternal transcripts during the MZT both temporally and mechanistically.
source: mRNA degradation is a key feature of early embryonic development, with the majority of the maternal transcriptome turned over and replaced by the zygotic transcriptome during the MZT. Founder granule-associated oskar degradation is distinct from degradation of unlocalized oskar, nanos, and other maternal transcripts during the MZT both temporally and mechanistically.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different timing and factor requirements.

claim: Degradation of oskar in the germ plasm occurs well in advance of pole cell formation.
source: Degradation of oskar in the germ plasm occurs well in advance of pole cell formation whereas the majority of MZT-related mRNA degradation occurs after pole cells have formed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oskar degradation begins at nc7 while pole cells form at nc10.

claim: The majority of MZT-related mRNA degradation occurs after pole cells have formed.
source: Degradation of oskar in the germ plasm occurs well in advance of pole cell formation whereas the majority of MZT-related mRNA degradation occurs after pole cells have formed.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and experimental data.

claim: oskar degradation in the germ plasm is mediated solely by maternal factors.
source: Consistent with this timing, oskar degradation in the germ plasm is mediated solely by maternal factors whereas oskar degradation in the bulk cytoplasm relies on both maternal and zygotic machineries (Thomsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oskar degradation in unfertilized eggs and citation to previous work.

claim: oskar degradation in the bulk cytoplasm relies on both maternal and zygotic machineries.
source: Consistent with this timing, oskar degradation in the germ plasm is mediated solely by maternal factors whereas oskar degradation in the bulk cytoplasm relies on both maternal and zygotic machineries (Thomsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Unlocalized oskar and nanos are degraded with the same kinetics during the MZT.
source: Unlocalized oskar and nanos are degraded with the same kinetics (Thomsen et al., 2010) and degradation factors (Laver et al., 2015a) during the MZT.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Unlocalized oskar and nanos are degraded by the same degradation factors during the MZT.
source: Unlocalized oskar and nanos are degraded with the same kinetics (Thomsen et al., 2010) and degradation factors (Laver et al., 2015a) during the MZT.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Only oskar is degraded in the germ plasm.
source: By contrast, only oskar is degraded in the germ plasm and this degradation does not require Brain tumor or Pumilio, but depends in part on Aubergine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oskar but not nanos or cyclin B degradation in the germ plasm.

claim: oskar degradation in the germ plasm does not require Brain tumor or Pumilio.
source: By contrast, only oskar is degraded in the germ plasm and this degradation does not require Brain tumor or Pumilio, but depends in part on Aubergine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing normal oskar degradation in brain tumor and pumilio mutants.

claim: oskar degradation in the germ plasm depends in part on Aubergine.
source: By contrast, only oskar is degraded in the germ plasm and this degradation does not require Brain tumor or Pumilio, but depends in part on Aubergine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing partial stabilization of oskar in aubergine mutants.

claim: Redirecting oskar to germ granules results in its stabilization, akin to nanos mRNA.
source: Moreover, redirecting oskar to germ granules results in its stabilization, akin to nanos mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing o∆gn stability.

claim: The differential susceptibility of oskar and germ granule mRNAs in the germ plasm is imparted by properties of the granules in which they reside.
source: These results, together with evidence that oskar degradation precedes founder granule disassembly, indicate that the differential suceptibility of oskar and germ granule mRNAs in the germ plasm is imparted by properties of the granules in which they reside.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence showing granule-specific degradation.

claim: The selective degradation of oskar among the hundreds of different mRNAs that share the germ plasm derives from the exclusive ability of founder granules to recruit decapping and degradation machinery.
source: The selective degradation of oskar among the hundreds of different mRNAs that share the germ plasm derives from the exclusive ability of founder granules to recruit decapping and degradation machinery.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that DCP1 associates with founder granules but not germ granules.

claim: Aubergine is a core germ granule protein.
source: The requirement for Aubergine in oskar degradation is itself surprising. First, Aubergine is a core germ granule protein and has been shown to stabilize germ granule mRNAs through an interaction with the poly(A) polymerase Wispy (Dufourt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: Aubergine has been shown to stabilize germ granule mRNAs through an interaction with the poly(A) polymerase Wispy.
source: The requirement for Aubergine in oskar degradation is itself surprising. First, Aubergine is a core germ granule protein and has been shown to stabilize germ granule mRNAs through an interaction with the poly(A) polymerase Wispy (Dufourt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Aubergine has been proposed to mediate degradation of mRNAs during the MZT by both piRNA-mediated cleavage and recruitment of Smaug and the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex.
source: Second, Aubergine has been proposed to mediate degradation of mRNAs during the MZT by both piRNA-mediated cleavage and recruitment of the RNA-binding protein Smaug and the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex (Barckmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: oskar degradation is Smaug-independent.
source: oskar degradation is Smaug-independent, however (Tadros et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Aubergine's requirement for association of DCP1 with founder granules suggests that piRNA-mediated degradation may not be the primary mode.
source: Whether Aubergine might also direct piRNA-mediated degradation of oskar in founder granules remains a question for future study but its requirement for association of DCP1 with founder granules suggests that piRNA-mediated degradation may not be the primary mode.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that Aubergine is required for DCP1 recruitment.

claim: Aubergine did not colocalize with founder granules.
source: Moreover, we did not detect colocalization of Aubergine with founder granules suggesting that Aubergine acts indirectly, perhaps by sequestering stability factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Aubergine acts indirectly in oskar degradation, perhaps by sequestering stability factors.
source: Moreover, we did not detect colocalization of Aubergine with founder granules suggesting that Aubergine acts indirectly, perhaps by sequestering stability factors.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the lack of colocalization.

claim: Cytoplasmic Aubergine might associate with founder granules only transiently or in small quantities.
source: Alternatively, cytoplasmic Aubergine might associate with founder granules only transiently or in small quantities.
evidence: This claim is speculative, offering an alternative explanation for lack of colocalization.

claim: The concentration of up to hundreds of oskar molecules in founder granules may enhance interaction of oskar with the decapping and degradation machinery, increasing reaction rates.
source: The concentration of up to hundreds of oskar molecules in founder granules may enhance interaction of oskar with the decapping and degradation machinery, increasing reaction rates so that the germ plasm load of oskar is sufficiently reduced prior to pole cell formation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for how compartmentalization enhances degradation.

claim: Founder granules create a hub, bringing the various components of the decapping and degradation machinery into close proximity.
source: Moreover, as non-membrane bound organelles, founder granules would create a hub, bringing the various components of the decapping and degradation machinery into close proximity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the properties of RNP granules.

claim: oskar RNA might regulate the properties of founder granules.
source: Our finding that founder granules are stabilized when oskar is stabilized, as in aubergine mutants, suggests that oskar RNA might regulate the properties of these granules, similarly to the role of RNA in dictating the physical properties of liquid droplets in vitro and in Ashbya cells in vivo (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between oskar and founder granule stability, with analogy to other systems.

claim: Under certain conditions, retrotransposon mRNAs can mimic oskar and localize to the germ plasm using the same transport machinery.
source: Interestingly, under certain conditions, retrotransposon mRNAs can mimic oskar and localize to the germ plasm using the same transport machinery (Tiwari et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Founder granules might sequester and destroy retrotransposon mRNAs in the germ plasm, preventing their reinsertion into the genome and thus maintaining genome integrity.
source: Founder granules might also therefore sequester and destroy retrotransposon mRNAs in the germ plasm, preventing their reinsertion into the genome and thus maintaining genome integrity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an additional function for founder granules.

claim: Germ granules provide the pole cells with a maternal endowment needed for germline development.
source: We suggest that whereas germ granules provide the pole cells with a maternal endowment needed for germline development, founder granules serve an opposing function to protect the germline from inheriting deleterious transcripts.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and inference from the data.

claim: Founder granules serve an opposing function to protect the germline from inheriting deleterious transcripts.
source: We suggest that whereas germ granules provide the pole cells with a maternal endowment needed for germline development, founder granules serve an opposing function to protect the germline from inheriting deleterious transcripts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing oskar toxicity and degradation in founder granules.
